content: Symptoms of a Serious Allergic Reaction Difficulty breathing or wheezing. A rapid or racing heartbeat. Fever or a general feeling of being unwell. Swollen lymph nodes. Swelling of the face, lips, mouth, tongue, or throat. Difficulty swallowing or a sensation of tightness in the throat. Itching, skin rash, or pale red bumps on the skin (hives). Nausea or vomiting. Dizziness, lightheadedness, or fainting. Stomach cramps. Joint pain. Antibiotic-Associated Diarrhea Overgrowth of a bacterium called Clostridioides difficile (C. diff) can occur in the gut when taking antibiotics, including dicloxacillin. This can lead to antibiotic-associated diarrhea, which may develop even up to two months after stopping the medication. Contact your healthcare provider immediately if you experience: Watery diarrhea. Persistent diarrhea that does not resolve. Blood in your stool. Severe stomach cramps. Fever that begins after starting or finishing the antibiotic. Seizures Some individuals taking dicloxacillin have reported seizures. Seizures can vary in type and may not always be easy to recognize. Stop taking dicloxacillin and contact your healthcare provider immediately if you experience: Muscle twitching, jerking, spasms, tremors, or other uncontrolled movements. Stiffness in your arms or legs. Feelings of anxiety, nervousness, confusion, or a sense of impending doom. Dizziness or lightheadedness. Fainting or loss of consciousness. Kidney Damage Dicloxacillin can cause kidney damage. Contact your healthcare provider immediately if you experience: Decreased need to urinate. Swelling in your feet, ankles, or legs. Weakness or unusual fatigue. Difficulty breathing or chest pain/pressure. Confusion. Nausea. Seizures. Blood Disorders Dicloxacillin can lead to blood disorders such as eosinophilia, hemolytic anemia, agranulocytosis, neutropenia, leukopenia, or bone marrow suppression. Stop taking dicloxacillin and seek medical attention immediately if you experience: Fever. Shortness of breath. Pale or yellowish skin. Easy bruising or bleeding. Frequent infections. Unusual weakness or fatigue. Dizziness, lightheadedness, or a feeling of faintness. Headache. Rapid or irregular heartbeat. Liver Damage Dicloxacillin can cause liver damage, also known as hepatotoxicity. Contact your healthcare provider immediately if you experience: Nausea or vomiting. Stomach or abdominal pain. Fever. Weakness or unusual fatigue. Itching. Loss of appetite. Light-colored stools. Dark-colored urine. Yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes (jaundice). Precautions: Who Should Not Use Dicloxacillin? Do not take dicloxacillin if you are allergic to: Dicloxacillin itself. Any of the ingredients in the specific product dispensed. Your pharmacist can provide a full list of ingredients. Important Information Before Using Dicloxacillin Take dicloxacillin on an empty stomach with a large glass of water (at least 4 ounces or 120 milliliters) at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal. Remain sitting or standing upright while taking dicloxacillin. Do not take it while lying down or right before going to bed. Only take dicloxacillin if it has been prescribed to you by a healthcare provider. Follow the prescribed dosage and instructions. Do not share dicloxacillin with others, even if they have the same condition, as it may harm them. Keep dicloxacillin out of reach of children. What to Tell Your Healthcare Provider Before Using Dicloxacillin Inform your healthcare provider about all your health conditions and any prescription or over-the-counter (OTC) medications, vitamins, minerals, herbal products, or supplements you are using. This will help them determine if dicloxacillin is appropriate for you. Specifically, discuss the following: Any allergies to penicillin or other medications. Asthma. Nausea, vomiting, or gastrointestinal issues. History of antibiotic-associated diarrhea. Kidney problems. Pregnancy: It is not known if dicloxacillin affects pregnancy or harms an unborn baby. Inform your provider if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Breastfeeding: Dicloxacillin passes into breast milk. Inform your provider if you are breastfeeding or planning to breastfeed. Drug Interactions Dicloxacillin is best absorbed on an empty stomach. Take it with a large glass of water at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals. It is unknown if alcohol affects dicloxacillin, but heavy drinking can weaken your immune response and make it harder for your body to fight infections. Always inform your healthcare provider about any prescription or OTC medications, vitamins, minerals, herbal products, or supplements you are using. Avoid taking additional medications without physician approval, including OTC products like antacids, laxatives, or vitamins. Discuss with your provider if you are using any of the following: Tetracyclines (e.g., tetracycline, doxycycline, minocycline, omadacycline, sarecycline). Probenecid (commonly used for gout). Warfarin (a blood thinner). Overdose If you or someone else has taken too much dicloxacillin, seek medical help immediately, call 911, or contact a Poison Control Center at 800-222-1222. Missed Dose If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and take only the next scheduled dose. Do not take double or extra doses. Complete the full prescribed course of dicloxacillin, even if your symptoms improve or resolve. This reduces the risk of future infections becoming resistant to dicloxacillin or similar antibiotics. Common Brand Names Dicloxacillin is sold under brand names such as Dycill, Dynapen, and Pathocil. Uses Dicloxacillin is an antibiotic used to treat bacterial infections caused by certain bacteria. It is not effective against viral infections (e.g., the common cold, influenza, or coronavirus) or non-bacterial infections. It may also be used for other conditions as determined by your healthcare provider. Mechanism of Action Dicloxacillin works by killing certain bacteria by preventing them from forming their cell walls. Dosage Forms Dicloxacillin is available as oral capsules in 250 mg and 500 mg strengths. Storage Store dicloxacillin at room temperature (68°F to 77°F or 20°C to 25°C). It can tolerate short-term exposure to temperatures between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C), such as during transport. Side Effects Common Side Effects Nausea. Vomiting. Diarrhea. Black, hairy tongue. Serious Side Effects Severe allergic reactions, antibiotic-associated diarrhea, seizures, kidney damage, blood disorders, and liver damage (as described above). Contact your healthcare provider if you suspect any serious side effects.
